newsitem.title: FRANCE: BoF's Marchelli would like Frenchman as ECB head.
newsitem.headline: BoF's Marchelli would like Frenchman as ECB head.

text.p: Bank of France council member Paul Marchelli suggested in an interview that a French person should be named as the first head of the European Central Bank.

"I would remind you that when Europe decided to put the headquarters of the European Central Bank (ECB) in Frankfurt, there was an unspoken commitment on the part of the Germans that the first head would be French," he said in an interview to be published in Saturday's edition of weekly magazine Investir.
"I hope people remember that when the time comes."

The comments by Marchelli, who is close to President Jacques Chirac, add to evidence that France may be determined to get its own candidate to run the future central bank after Europe launches its single currency in January 1999.
Chirac said in December that France would not necessarily accept Dutch central bank head Wim Duisenberg, tipped as the favourite for the job, as the head of the ECB.
Duisenberg is due to become head of the European Monetary Institute -- the ECB's forerunner -- in July 1997.

Marchelli also repeated that he favoured a strong political power to counterbalance the future ECB, echoing comments made by Chirac, and also suggested that national central banks should have some input in influencing ECB policy.

He argued that in 1999, countries would cede control of monetary policy to the ECB, while fiscal policy would be constrained by a European Union budget stability pact agreed at a summit in Dublin in December.
The only economic lever left to politicians would be employment and wages.
"It is a major problem. That is why I am in favour of a strong economic and social government opposite the European Central Bank.

"I would also like the Bank of France's monetary policy council to have, for at least several years, the ability -- I would even say the duty -- to give advice to France's representative at the European Central Bank. Which would imply a reform of the Maastricht treaty," he added.
Marchelli repeated that he would like to see a stronger dollar, but said "the current trend is a good start."
